news_drafts.headline: Pembrokeshire social care overspent £6.521m in the year; council as a whole underspent by £2.0m
news_drafts.lead:
Pembrokeshire County Council's social care services spent £6.521m more than budgeted in the year, but the council as a whole finished £2.0m under budget. Figures in an appendix to the Governance and Audit Committee's papers for 6 October show the overspend was offset by underspends elsewhere.

Children's Services accounts for most of it, with an overspend of £5.649m. Adult Services overspent by £0.872m. Together they make up the £6.521m. The appendix sets out the position in the council's outturn (the actual figures for the year once it has ended, as against what was budgeted).

Other services spent less than planned and covered the gap. Infrastructure underspent by £1.977m, and Education also finished under budget. The net result across the council was the £2.0m underspend. The figures in the appendix are the council's own and are presented by service, with no explanation of the causes of the social care overspends.

news_drafts.headline: Pembrokeshire puts 92% of second homes council tax premium into its budget, with a £23.3m gap for 2027-28
news_drafts.lead:
Pembrokeshire County Council puts 92% of the money raised from its council tax premium on second homes into its general budget, Cabinet papers for 5 October show. The premium is the extra charge the council applies on top of standard council tax for second homes. In 2026-27, £9.008m of it goes to general fund services, the council's main day-to-day spending account.

The money pays for core services, including homelessness (£2.05m), schools (£4.71m) and public realm maintenance. The paper says the premium therefore covers parts of those services that would otherwise have to be paid for from other sources of day-to-day spending.

That matters because the council projects a funding gap of £23.3m for 2027-28, the shortfall between what it expects to spend and what it expects to have. The council's Director of Resources sets out what changing the premium would do to that gap. The paper says: "Based on the current allocation of 92% of the second homes Council Tax premium income to the Council's budget relating to affordable housing and enhancing the sustainability of local communities, a 25% decrease in the premium would increase the funding gap for 2027-28 by circa. £1.4m". A 25% change in the premium level would move the gap by about £1.4m either way.

findings.headline: 490-home housing programme 2024-32 dependent on continued second homes premium funding
findings.detail: The HRA business plan includes 490 homes planned, under construction, or built between 2024-25 and 2031-32 through both direct council build and grant support to partners (Solva CLT, Homebuy scheme). The council allocated £5.5m from the premium reserve in 2025-26 for housing development. Future programme delivery is explicitly dependent on ongoing availability of grant support from second homes premium revenue.
findings.matters: Housing delivery is a stated council priority; a lender assesses whether capital plans are executable. The dependence on discretionary premium revenue which has already been cut (150% to 125%) creates execution risk for the housing programme.
findings.figures: 490 homes planned 2024-25 to 2031-32; £5.5 million allocated 2025-2026 from second homes premium reserve
findings.quote: Future developments are dependent on availability of grant support (including second homes premium) and in total, between 2024-25 through to 2031-32 a total of 490 homes are either planned, under construction or built.

findings.headline: Holiday let numbers fell 30% after Valuation Office backlog cleared in October 2024; further reclassifications likely as backlog remains
findings.detail: The 182-day letting threshold for holiday let exemption changed in April 2023, but administrative backlog at the Valuation Office prevented reclassification until October 2024, when holiday let numbers suddenly fell 30%. The Valuation Office backlog for reviews and appeals remains, and Welsh Government is consulting on whether to reduce the threshold further, creating ongoing uncertainty in the council's tax base.
findings.matters: Tax base volatility makes revenue forecasting unreliable; properties reclassifying between non-domestic rates and council tax affect which properties are subject to premiums, creating further uncertainty in discretionary premium income that the council now depends on for core services.
findings.figures: 30% fall in holiday lets after October 2024; backlog partially cleared; some properties transferred from NDR (non-domestic rates) to council tax as second homes
findings.quote: Although the 182-day actual letting threshold change was made on 1 April 2023, the number of holiday lets remained largely unchanged until October 2024 after which the total number of holiday lets fell by 30%.

findings.headline: Solva Community Land Trust affordable housing project has experienced significant delays; 18 homes approved December 2019 not yet delivered as of March 2026
findings.detail: The project was approved in principle December 2019 with a target completion date of summer 2021. Grant funding was formally committed from the second homes premium reserve in October 2020. As of March 2026 report, the project remains undelivered with significant delays; the council is restructuring the arrangement and the developer awaits planning permission for additional units.
findings.matters: Capital delivery delays signal execution risk in the council's housing programme; this project relied on discretionary premium funding that is now at risk given premium rate reductions. A lender assesses whether the council can deliver promised housing stock.
findings.figures: 18 affordable houses; approved December 2019; grant committed 5 October 2020; March 2026 status report
findings.quote: On 5 October 2020 Cabinet authorised the award of a grant from the Second Homes Council Tax fund to Ateb Housing Association (working alongside Solva Community Land Trust) 18 new affordable houses.  Since then there have been significant delays.

findings.headline: £33.5m annually from second homes and empty homes premiums allocated to general fund budget since 2024-25, planned to continue through medium term
findings.detail: The council has structured its budget to allocate premium revenue directly to core services: homelessness (£2.05m), schools (£4.71m), public realm maintenance (£1.15m), youth services (£0.9m). This arrangement is planned to continue through 2027-28 and the medium term, creating structural dependence on discretionary revenue streams.
findings.matters: This creates material revenue risk: if premium rates fall further or if second homes/empty homes properties decline in number, core service budgets face pressure. A lender needs to understand whether the general fund budget is sustainable if premium income reduces.
findings.figures: £33.5m allocated since 2024-25; homelessness £2,050k; schools £4,708k; public realm £1,150k
findings.quote: Since 2024-25 £33.5m has been allocated to the general fund budget in respect of elements of the budget relating to affordable housing and enhancing the sustainability of local communities and it is proposed that this arrangement will continue in 2027-28 and over the medium term.

findings.headline: Second homes council tax premium reduced from 150% to 125% in 2026-27, with tourism industry impact cited as main reason
findings.detail: The council deliberately reduced the premium rate in October 2025, marking the second rate change in three years (100% in 2022-23, 200% in 2024-25, now 125%). The reduction explicitly acknowledges tourism industry concerns as the primary driver of the policy shift, showing the council is balancing revenue objectives against economic pressure.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess whether the council's revenue forecasts account for lower premium yield; a peer council wants to understand how to navigate competing policy priorities (housing affordability vs. economic resilience).
findings.quote: It is clear from Council's October 2025 minutes when it decided to reduce the second home council tax premium rate from 150% to 125%, that one of the main reasons was the potential impact on the tourism industry.

daily_post.headline: West Wales region continuing to experience high levels of delayed hospital discharges affecting emergency care capacity
daily_post.lead: Delayed hospital discharge typically reflects adult social care capacity constraints; this can drive future service cost pressures and demand volatility, affecting council financial planning and resilience.
